Apply for your key · Brief · API docs · Starter kit · Build page · Results · Discord

You are the procurement team of Hollerau Pumpenwerke, a fictional German pump maker, and the inbox is full: a foundry wants +9.5 %, a framework contract expires, a new pump needs three quotes. Build an **AI buyer agent** that reads the company's data, negotiates by e-mail with our supplier bots, and closes the best total deal, or walks away. Practise all weekend against our hosted suppliers. On Sunday at 12:00 a Live Final on hidden cases ranks every team. This repo holds everything you need: the brief, the API docs, a Python starter kit and the data package. Bring your own LLM, any provider; we run the suppliers. ## Start in 15 minutes You need Python 3.12, [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) and git. 1. **Apply.** Open **https://arena.tacto.ai/apply** and enter your team name and a contact e-mail. Tip: start the name with one emoji, it shows on the big screen. 2. **Show your match code at the Tacto desk.** We approve. 3. **Copy your key.** It appears **once** on the page you applied on; then press "Got the key". One key per team. Lost it? We reset it at the desk. 4. **Run the four commands.** ```bash git clone https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit.git cd negotiation-arena-kit/starter-kit cp .env.example .env # paste your key: ARENA_API_KEY=... uv sync --all-extras # install uv run arena me # your team and its practice quota uv run arena play case:P01 # the naive example agent negotiates one practice case uv run arena board # your team on the practice leaderboard ``` `arena play` prints the deal, your score and a replay link: every e-mail and the supplier's reasons in words. Read it, improve your agent, play again. Next steps, the LLM agent and your own agent: [starter-kit/README.md](starter-kit/README.md). ## Links | What | Where | |---|---| | Apply for your key | https://arena.tacto.ai/apply | | Brief: story, task, score, rules | [brief/brief.md](brief/brief.md) | | API docs | [brief/api.md](brief/api.md) | | Starter kit: client, example agents, Live Final runner, local simulator, MCP server | [starter-kit/](starter-kit/) | | Submission and pitch | [brief/submission.md](brief/submission.md) | | Practice build page: every team's quota, records and highlights | https://arena.tacto.ai/live | | Live Final results, team by team and case by case | https://arena.tacto.ai/results | | Questions | Discord https://discord.gg/hPwFfbWRV · the Tacto table | ## The weekend at a glance | When | What | |---|---| | Sat 10:00 | Kickoff and reveal: brief, data, kit and practice arena go live | | Sat 12:00-13:00 | **Deep dive**, ground floor (room on the signs): data, API, kit, Q&A. Bring a laptop. Challenge selection closes 13:00 | | Sat afternoon | Office hours at the Tacto table. Practice all weekend: 200 sessions per team per 24 hours | | Sat evening | We post on Discord when Tacto goes offline for the night | | Sun 08:00 | **New market data.** Run `uv run arena data` again; hidden cases may cite it | | Sun 09:00 | Pre-flight: one practice case through your final setup | | Sun 12:00 | **Code freeze**, submit on ehl.gg. **Live Final**: five waves, 8 minutes each, every team at once | | Sun 13:00 | **Top 10 pitch** to the Tacto jury: 5 minutes + 2 minutes of questions | | Sun 14:30 | Track winners and the two finalists announced | | Sun 15:30 | Grand Final pitches (AudiMax) | | Sun 16:30 | Awards | ## Rules that matter - **No human in the loop** during the Live Final. They are for you, not for your agent. - **One key per team.** No attacks on the service or on other teams. - Everything else counts, including weaknesses you find in our suppliers. Every replay is open to the jury. All rules: [brief, section 7](brief/brief.md#7-rules). ## What to submit on ehl.gg by Sun 12:00 - **Your repo** with the agent and a README that says how to run it, and the **commit hash** your agent runs in the final. The jury and tum.ai must be able to open it. - **A short description** of your approach. - **Slides** for the pitch. The top 10 pitch from 13:00. Details: [brief/submission.md](brief/submission.md). ## Prizes 1st place €1,500 · medals for the top 3 · the best 2 EHL finalist teams in this track go on to the Grand Final. ⟦Q2: how the Live Final score and the jury combine for places 1-3⟧ ## What is in this repo | Folder | What | |---|---| | [`brief/`](brief/) | The brief, the API docs, the submission guide | | [`starter-kit/`](starter-kit/) | Python client, a naive and an LLM example agent, the Live Final runner, `arena-sim` (the API on your laptop), an MCP server over the data | | [`data/`](data/) | Data package v1: CSV, SQLite, `facts.json`, contracts, letters, notes. Tacto · AI for industrial procurement · EHL Grand Finale 2026, Garching

# brief - `brief.md` - the participant brief (max. 4 pages) - `api.md` - the HTTP API reference - `submission.md` - what to submit on Sunday, and how the pitch works # Tacto Negotiation Arena - Participant brief > **Build an AI buyer agent that negotiates by e-mail with tough, realistic industrial suppliers, > gets the best total deal - and can explain how it got there.** ## 1. The story You are the procurement team of **Hollerau Pumpenwerke GmbH**, a fictional German pump maker: centrifugal pumps for buildings, water and industry, about €250M revenue, 900 people, one plant in Bavaria. Your team buys the parts of the pump line - castings, machined parts, sheet metal, seals, motors, fasteners, stainless bar - from about 45 suppliers. Today is **30 September 2026**, and the inbox is full: a foundry announces +9.5% on volute casings "due to energy and wages", a framework contract expires, a new pump series needs three quotes, a supplier with a red scorecard has to fix its quality. You answer the way buyers do: by e-mail. On the other side sit our **supplier bots**, each with a small team of **roles** behind it - the sales rep or owner who writes to you, a boss who must approve bigger moves, and engineering, quality, logistics, finance or legal, who answer their topics and attach documents. Tacto is the AI for industrial procurement: it gives procurement teams the intelligence to source every part at the best possible terms with minimal effort. Your company runs on that kind of data - orders, deliveries, invoices, contracts, scorecards, market indices, should-cost estimates, notes from supplier calls. Your job is to build the agent that turns this data into better deals. (In Tacto's product, agents such as the Defender Agent or the Sourcing Agent do parts of this job.) ## 2. The task Each **case** is one negotiation: a trigger (a letter, an expiring contract, an RFQ), your case file (need, goal, rates, must-haves, your alternative) and one to three supplier bots. Your **buyer agent** 1. **prepares** - reads the case file and mines the data package; 2. **negotiates by e-mail** - plain-language messages with up to three **term sheets** (alternative packages), the data IDs your arguments rest on, and attachments if you like; 3. **closes** - accepts one supplier term sheet, or walks away. **How a supplier decides.** Each supplier is a company with its own economics and a person at the desk - a family foundry that remembers how you treated it, a group with an approval ladder, a job shop that needs cash and work, a near-monopolist that barely moves. Its hard limits come from its own situation: it never sells below its cost floor, bigger moves need the boss's approval, data you cite is checked by ID, and it gives nothing without a move from you. Inside those limits it decides as that person would - reading your whole e-mail: the term sheets, the data, and what you signal (questions, arguments, threats, appreciation, urgency). It reacts to tone and relationship as people do; padding does not buy price. **Data is not automatically rewarded.** True data can disarm a supplier ("we didn't know that") - or meet "that's not our reality", because something else weighs more for it right now. The traces are in the data: call notes, letters, news, the remarks on its quotes. The skill is reading the supplier, not stacking evidence - and finding the trade it wants: a supplier short of cash may care more about when it is paid than about the price; one that cannot touch its list price may still move on other terms. ## 3. What you get (Sat 10:00) | What | Where | |---|---| | This brief, the API docs (`api.md`) and the submission guide (`submission.md`) | `https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit`, folder `brief/` | | **Data package v1**: CSV, the same data as SQLite, `facts.json` (every citable ID with the values the arena checks), contracts, letters, e-mails, meeting and call notes - the data behind all 19 practice cases | `https://arena.tacto.ai/v1/data/package.zip`, or the repo's `data/` | | **Practice arena**: 10 hosted practice cases, picked so every case type shows up; a replay after every case; practice leaderboard; a **sandbox** with 3 demo suppliers | `https://arena.tacto.ai` with your team's key - apply at `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply` (below) | | **Starter kit**: Python client, a naive agent, an LLM agent that writes e-mails and reads the attached documents, the Live Final runner, an MCP server over the data, `arena-sim` - the API on your laptop | the repo's `starter-kit/` - first agent on the board in 15 minutes | You bring your own LLM access; we only run the suppliers. Data and docs are CC BY 4.0, code MIT. **Your key - one per team.** Open `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply`, enter your team name and a contact e-mail, and show the match code it displays at the Tacto desk. Once we approve, the key appears **once** on that page: copy it, press "Got the key". Only that page shows it; lost it - we reset it. Tip: your team name may start with one emoji - it shows on the big screen (optional; nothing offensive). **Practice quota: 200 practice sessions per team per rolling 24 hours.** `GET /v1/me` shows what you have used and when it frees up. The build page `https://arena.tacto.ai/live` shows every team's quota use, practice records and highlights from Sat 10:00 to Sun 12:00. **`arena-sim`** speaks the arena's API exactly, with one plain scripted supplier: get your plumbing right there. It teaches the contract, not the suppliers - and we don't hand out our suppliers. Want a local opponent? Build your own supplier simulator from the public data: thinking into how real suppliers act is part of the challenge. **The learning loop:** play a practice case, read your exact score and its cost breakdown, open the replay - every e-mail and the supplier's reasons in words, as a real supplier would give them - improve your agent, play again. Your best score per practice case counts. ## 4. The data The buyer's world: supplier and part master data; three years of orders, goods receipts, invoices and payments; quality notifications and quarterly scorecards (on-time delivery, PPM); framework contracts and clauses; past RFQs and quotes; forecasts; supplier intel and news; past negotiations, letters, e-mails, meeting and call notes; should-cost estimates; spend down to the long tail; and monthly market indices (real public series, frozen at 2026-09-30). - **Every fact you can cite has an ID** `:[@period]`, e.g. `po:4500010001-10`, `idx:PPI-C2451@2026-08`, `sc:70110@2026Q3`, `ctr:4600070110#3.1`, `doc:…`. - What moves a supplier is in the data - some of it only in the notes and e-mails. Some notes are just noise. The company and its suppliers are fictional. - **Sunday 08:00: a second release** - market news, supplier letters and a memo from early October (`GET /v1/data` lists it). Hidden cases may cite its facts. Your agent should read it. ## 5. How a negotiation works - **Round 0:** every supplier sends its quote e-mail at once, with a quote PDF. - **Your message:** subject, body, up to 3 term sheets (each with a value for every negotiable field), the data IDs you rely on (IDs written in the body count too), optional text attachments. - **The supplier answers by e-mail:** the role in charge writes; its standing term sheet; a status - `open`, `final_offer` (push further and it may walk), `agreed` (it offers exactly your terms; you still accept), `walked_away`, `no_bid`; signals (reply delay, quote validity); fields it left out; and how each data argument checked out. A supplier's reply can take **up to about a minute**; its time never counts against your 60 seconds. - **Only you close a deal**, by accepting a supplier's standing term sheet. In **RFQ cases** 2-3 suppliers run in parallel threads; accepting one ends the case. - **Limits:** a round limit per thread (default 10 messages) and **60 seconds per message**, counted from the supplier's reply. A late message counts as a timeout: your last offer repeated, the supplier's patience drops; three in a row, or one after the last round, end the thread. - **Unstated terms default to the supplier's standard terms** - listed in its quote PDF. **Documents** are rendered from the supplier's data, never invented: the quote PDF (read it before you accept), a cost breakdown XLSX (ask; an open supplier sends one), an 8D report (quality), a delivery schedule XLSX (logistics), and the order confirmation at the deal. **What counts:** **term sheets bind** - nothing else. **Data you cite is checked**: the reply says `verified`, `contradicted` (a wrong figure or an unknown ID - it costs trust), `irrelevant` or `duplicate`; whether a true argument moves the supplier, and how far, is the supplier's business. **What you write is understood** - and has consequences, as it would with a person. ## 6. The score: total cost in € Only the accepted term sheet scores. The case values it as the **total cost C** of covering your **fixed need over a fixed horizon**, at the case's published rates. Every case states its **category goal** - `stabilise`, `secure_supply`, `quality_first`, `leverage` or `routine` - and its rates follow it. Reaching the goal is the skill. | Part of C | How | |---|---| | Price | committed units × unit price; units bought before a new price takes effect at the current price | | Uncovered need | need the deal does not cover at the fallback price, plus the goal's fallback risk on it | | Payment, freight, lead time | interest for paying earlier than your reference; freight by Incoterm; € per day beyond your need | | Quality, other | expected defects at the committed PPM minus chargebacks; tooling; an index clause on the case's index path, plus the goal's index risk | | The supplier's health | strategic and bottleneck goals only: € for every margin point the deal leaves the supplier below a sustainable margin (its margin on the cash it gets) | **Case score = (C_open − C_deal) / (C_open − C_best)**, clipped to 0…1. **C_open** is the best opening quote. **C_best** is the cheaper of the best package any supplier in the case would ever accept, with every valid lever applied, and your alternative - fixed per case, so good arguments raise your score instead of moving the yardstick. **No deal** scores your alternative (0 if none); some cases are best left without a deal. **A broken must-have** scores 0. **In the final** each wave scores 0-100 (the mean of its case scores × 100, one decimal) and your **points so far** are the sum of your wave scores - up to 500 after five waves. The formula is in `api.md`; `arena_kit.total_cost` computes C. **Example** (a `leverage` case: 3 % fallback risk) - need 4,000 a year for 2 years, interest 8%, reference 60 days. The foundry asks €43.20 for a 24-month contract at 30 days net. | | Terms | C | |---|---|---| | C_open | €43.20, 30 days: 8,000 × 43.20 = 345,600, plus 30 days of early payment at 8% = 2,304 | €347,904 | | Your deal | €41.60, 60 days: 8,000 × 41.60 = 332,800 | €332,800 | | C_best (hidden) | €40.80, 90 days: 326,400, minus 30 days of interest saved = 2,176 | €324,224 | | **Score** | (347,904 − 332,800) / (347,904 − 324,224) | **0.64** | The same €41.60 for 12 months covers half your need; the rest counts at the fallback price, say €46.00, plus 3 %: C = €355,920 - worse than the opening, score 0. ## 7. Base URL: `https://arena.tacto.ai/v1`. Every call except `/v1/data`, `/health` and the leaderboards needs your team's key in the header `X-API-Key`. The starter kit wraps all of this in `arena_kit.ArenaClient`. To try the API on your laptop, run `arena-sim` from the starter kit: the same API with one plain scripted supplier - it teaches the contract, not the suppliers. **Safe retries:** send a fresh `X-Move-Id` header (any unique string) with every `POST`. If the network drops, repeat the request with the same `X-Move-Id`: the arena returns the answer it already gave instead of acting twice. Reusing an id for a different request is a `422`. A request body may be at most 64 KB. Get it on the page `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply`: enter your team name and a contact e-mail, show the match code the page displays at the Tacto desk, and once an organiser approves, the key appears **once** on that page - copy it and press "Got the key". Only that page (or its link) shows the key; lost it → ask the organisers to reset it (the old key stops at once). Send the key as `X-API-Key` with every call. A missing or unknown key is a `401`; a paused or revoked key gets `403 "this key is paused - ask the organisers"` (or `revoked`) on every call. Returns the supplier's reply, a Message. With an `action`, it closes the case and returns the [result](#result-trace-and-back-office): `{"type": "accept", "term_sheet_id": "offer:…"}` takes that supplier's standing term sheet; `{"type": "walk_away"}` ends the case without a deal. (Offline wording from a local run; on the hosted arena the supplier writes its own e-mail and may well decide differently.) ## What counts **Term sheets bind** - nothing else. They are taken exactly as you send them, never guessed from prose; the deal is the term sheet you accept. **Data you cite is checked.** Cite the data by ID (in the body or in `refs`) and write your figure in the same sentence; the arena checks it against the data package (`facts.json`) and reports each check in the reply's `claim_results` - at most 3 per message, so write one argument per sentence. Order lines of different parts are separate arguments, so citing orders for three parts uses all three. Without a figure, the data's own value is taken. IDs of meeting notes, suppliers or parts are context, not checks. | You cite | Checked | Your figure | |---|---|---| | 2 × `idx`, one series, ≤ 12 months apart, ending within the last 12 months of the data | the change `(later / earlier − 1) × 100` | a % | | a `quote` of this case (in its `refs` or your alternative), or another supplier's `offer` in this session | its price, same part | EUR | | `sc` rows (quality also `qn`) | the mean on-time delivery, or the mean ppm if you speak of quality | a % / ppm | | 2-8 × `po`, same part | the order prices | - | | `fc` / `cost` / `news` | the recorded change / the estimate / that it is about this supplier | a % / EUR / - | | a letter `doc` giving notice + the contract `ctr` | the notice the letter gives, against the contract's | days | Tolerance: ±0.5 percentage points for %, else ±0.5 % (at least 0.01). Results: `verified` - the data matches; whether and how far it moves the supplier is the supplier's business. `irrelevant` - true, but not about this supplier or part, or an index window too long or too old. `contradicted` - an unknown ID or a wrong figure: it costs trust. `duplicate` - each ID counts once per case, except a rival's quote: in an RFQ you may cite it to every other bidder, and it counts once per supplier. Citing a buyer-private fact - a rival quote - reveals it to the supplier you cite it to. **Verified is not the same as convincing.** A supplier's hard limits come from its own economics and authority: its cost floor, its boss's approval for bigger moves, no concession without a move from you. Inside them it decides as the person it is. True data may disarm it, move it a little, or meet "that's not our reality" because something else weighs more for it right now - its notes, letters, news and quote remarks show what. Identical messages need not get identical replies. **What you write is understood** - questions, arguments, signals of urgency or of having no alternative, a budget, threats, appreciation, tone, attempts to manipulate - and has consequences, as it would with a person. Questions go to the person in charge, who answers as openly as the company is. Cheaper engineering variants a supplier mentions are information, not binding terms. ## Documents Rendered from the supplier's structured state - never written by a language model, byte-stable. | Document | When | What matters | |---|---|---| | Quote PDF | opening e-mail; with `final_offer` and `agreed` | offered terms, **the standard terms that apply to everything not stated**, terms fixed by your enquiry, validity | | Cost breakdown XLSX | you asked and the supplier is open enough | elements in EUR per unit and their share (formulas) | | 8D report PDF | quality topics | scorecards, the 8D steps, a ppm commitment | | Delivery schedule XLSX | delivery and capacity topics | monthly quantities, lead time | | Order confirmation PDF | at the deal | the agreed terms | ## Terms Every term with € weight is a structured field. A term sheet carries **exactly** the case's `negotiable` fields; `fixed_terms` hold the rest. Every negotiable field except `unit_price` takes a value from `term_options` (or the supplier's standard value). | Field | Type | Meaning | |---|---|---| | `unit_price` | number, € with 2 decimals, per the part's `price_unit` | price | | `payment_days` | int, 0-120 | days net | | `lead_time_days` | int | order to delivery | | `volume_per_year` | int | binding annual units | | `contract_months` | int, 0-36 | 0 = a single order (counts as one year's lot) | | `effective_date` | ISO date | from when the new price applies | | `index_clause` | null or `{series, material_share, deadband_pct, base_month}` | the price follows an index | | `incoterm` | `EXW`, `FCA`, `DAP` | freight per unit from the case file | | `tooling_eur` | € | one-off | | `ppm_commitment` | int | committed defect rate | | `chargeback_eur_per_complaint` | € | what the supplier pays per complaint | ## Case file Case files come through the API, not in the data package: `GET /v1/cases?set=practice|sandbox` any time, `GET /v1/cases?set=final` wave by wave. | Field | | |---|---| | `case_id`, `set`, `type` | `type`: `price_increase`, `renewal`, `rfq`, `bundling`, `raw_material`, `capacity`, `quality` | | `title`, `briefing` | the situation, in prose | | `trigger_doc` | the document that started it, e.g. the supplier's letter | | `parts`, `suppliers` | what is negotiated, with whom (2-3 suppliers = an RFQ) | | `negotiable`, `fixed_terms`, `term_options` | see [Terms](#terms) | | `buyer` | your need and rates, below | | `round_limit` | your messages per thread, default 10 | | `refs` | data the case points to - a start, not the whole story | | `facts` | hidden cases: facts that exist only in this case (e.g. a new letter), in the format of `facts.json`, citable in this case | `buyer`: | Field | | |---|---| | `need_per_year`, `horizon_years` | the need the deal should cover, and over how many years (≤ 3) | | `current_unit_price` | what you pay until a new price takes effect | | `fallback_unit_price` | what uncovered need costs (re-tender or spot, incl. switching) | | `interest_rate`, `reference_payment_days` | your cost of money per year; your standard payment term | | `need_lead_time_days`, `late_cost_per_day` | the lead time you need; € per day beyond it | | `cost_per_defect` | € per defective part | | `category_goal` | `stabilise` (strategic), `secure_supply` (bottleneck), `quality_first`, `leverage` or `routine` - the company's category strategy for this part; the briefing says it in words, and the rates in this block follow it | | `fallback_risk_pct` | % added to what uncovered need costs: buying it later is a risk | | `index_risk_pct` | % of the indexed spend: the risk you carry with an index clause | | `sustainable_margin_pct`, `relationship_eur_per_point` | `stabilise` and `secure_supply` only: the margin a healthy supplier needs, and € per margin point and year that a deal leaves it below | | `freight_eur_per_unit` | `{EXW, FCA, DAP}` | | `index_paths` | `{series: change}` - the expected index move over the horizon, `0.04` = +4% | | `must_haves` | `[{field, op, value}]`, `op` one of `<=`, `>=`, `<`, `>`, `==`, `!=`; a deal that breaks one scores 0 | | `alternative` | `{kind: none \| quote \| current_contract, ref, terms}` - what you get without a deal | ## Data IDs IDs have the form `:[@period]`, are unique across the package and sit in the first column of each table. `facts.json` in the package lists every citable ID with the values the arena checks: | ID | Fields | |---|---| | `idx:@YYYY-MM` | `series`, `month`, `value` | | `quote:` | `part`, `supplier`, `unit_price` (+ the quote's other terms) | | `sc:@YYYYQn` | `supplier`, `otd_pct`, `ppm` | | `qn:` | `supplier`, `part`, `ppm` | | `po:` | `supplier`, `part`, `unit_price` | | `cost:` | `part`, `unit_cost` | | `fc:@YYYY-MM` | `part`, `change_pct` | | `news:` | `supplier` (or null) | | `doc:` | `supplier`, `date`, `days` (notice given), `asked_price` (price letters) | | `ctr:` | `supplier`, `days` (notice agreed) | Offers made in the session are citable as `offer:` IDs. ## Result, trace and back office Closing returns the result (without the trace); `GET /v1/sessions/{sid}` adds the trace after the end - in the final after the final. The numbers are exact in every set: your score, `c_open`, `c_best` and the cost breakdown, relationship charge included. | Field | | |---|---| | `ended`, `deal`, `must_haves_ok` | | | `supplier_id`, `offer_id`, `terms` | who and what you closed - fields the term sheet left out filled with the supplier's standard terms | | `c_open`, `c_deal`, `c_alt`, `c_best` | see [Cost and score](#cost-and-score); `c_alt` is your alternative | | `score` | 0-1 | | `cost_breakdown` | `c_deal` by part: price, uncovered_need, fallback_risk, payment_terms, freight, late_delivery, quality, tooling, index_clause, index_risk, relationship | | `trace` | after the end (final: after the final), per move, in every set: `{round, actor, move, reasons}` - `move` is the e-mail as sent with its terms, status and claim results, `reasons` the supplier's reasons in words (figures it keeps to itself shown as `…`) | ## Cost and score With `N` = `need_per_year`, `H` = `horizon_years`, `V` = `volume_per_year`, `M` = `contract_months`, `P` = `unit_price`, `r` = `interest_rate`, `d_ref` = `reference_payment_days`: ``` years = min(M / 12, H); a single order (M = 0) counts as 1 a commitment beyond the horizon committed = V · years neither costs nor earns covered = min(V, N) · years pre = units bought between the horizon start and effective_date (at current_unit_price) new = (committed − pre) · P bought at the new price spend = pre · current_unit_price + new uncovered = (N · H − covered) · fallback_unit_price C = spend + uncovered · (1 + fallback_risk_pct / 100) uncovered need, and its risk + spend · r · (d_ref − payment_days) / 360 paying earlier costs interest + committed · freight_eur_per_unit[incoterm] + late_cost_per_day · max(0, lead_time_days − need_lead_time_days) + committed · ppm_commitment / 1e6 · (cost_per_defect − min(chargeback_eur_per_complaint, cost_per_defect)) + tooling_eur + new · material_share · max(0, |index_path| − deadband_pct / 100) · sign(index_path) with an index clause + new · material_share · index_risk_pct / 100 with an index clause + relationship_eur_per_point · soft(sustainable_margin_pct − supplier_margin_pct) · years stabilise and secure_supply only soft(g) = 0 for g ≤ 0; g² / 10 for 0 < g ≤ 5; g − 2.5 for g > 5 (margin points: gentle, no kink) ``` The horizon starts at the fixed or earliest `effective_date` option; `index_path` is the case's expected move of the clause's series. **The supplier's margin** is `(value − full_cost) / value × 100`: `full_cost` is the supplier's full cost per unit, `value` what the deal is worth to it in cash per unit - the price at its own standard terms that would pay it the same: the price (units sold before the new price applies at the current price), payment timing and tooling paid up front at what money is worth to **it** now (more to a supplier short of cash), the freight leg it carries, chargebacks at the defect rate it really has, and what a faster delivery, a larger volume or a tighter defect commitment costs or brings it. A longer contract or an index clause is security for it, not cash, and does not count. So a cash-short supplier that trades a lower price for faster payment is not squeezed. You don't know its cost and rates - estimate them (should-cost data, its quotes, what it tells you). `arena_kit.total_cost(case, terms, standard, supplier)` computes C, with `arena_kit.cost.supplier_value` for your estimate of the supplier. ``` score = clip((C_open − C_deal) / (C_open − C_best), 0, 1) ``` `C_open`: the cheapest opening quote (among those that keep the must-haves). `C_best`: the cheaper of your alternative and the best package any supplier in the case would accept with every valid lever applied. No deal scores the alternative (0 if none); a broken must-have scores 0; if `C_open − C_best` ≤ €0.01, a deal at `C_best` scores 1. Team total = mean case score × 100. ## Live Final in waves The hidden cases come in 5 themed waves. The host introduces each wave on the big screen, then starts it; a wave holds several cases that appear at its start, for every team at the same moment. Before a wave starts, the API names nothing of it - not its theme, its cases or how many there are: `GET /v1/cases?set=final` answers `403` until the first wave starts, and a session on a case of a wave not started yet is a `404 "no such case"`, like any unknown ID. Once waves have started, the list holds the case files of every started wave, each with four more fields: | Field | | |---|---| | `wave`, `theme` | the wave's number and the theme the host revealed | | `open` | `true` while the wave runs; you can open sessions for its cases only then (after its end: `403 " belongs to wave , which is not running"`) | | `seconds_left` | until the wave's cap - 8 minutes for every wave (the host may extend one); read it, don't assume it | Inside a wave, each team gets the cases in its own order. One session per case; a second `POST /v1/sessions` is a `409` naming the running session - pick it up with `GET /v1/sessions/{sid}` and `GET …/threads/{supplier_id}`. **At the cap every session of the wave still open ends without a deal** (`end_reason: wave_cap`, the alternative's score); later calls get a `409`. Each wave scores 0-100 for your team; the board adds them up as your points so far. Poll the case list every few seconds and keep your agent running until the last wave has closed - `arena run --set final` in the starter kit does this. ## Time, errors and limits - **60 seconds per message**, per thread, counted from the supplier's reply. A message later than that counts as a timeout: your last offer is repeated and the supplier's patience drops (`409`, the answer is in the thread). Three timeouts in a row, or one after the last round, end the thread. - **A supplier's reply can take up to about a minute** - its time never counts against your 60 seconds. Use an HTTP timeout of at least 180 s (the kit uses 180). - **Limits per key:** 10 calls per second, 10 open sessions. A Live Final wave holds several cases that appear at its start and gives you 8 minutes: play them all in parallel. | Status | When | |---|---| | `401` | missing or unknown `X-API-Key` | | `403` | paused or revoked key; a practice case that is not hosted; `POST /v1/register` (keys come from `/apply`); the final's case list before the first wave; a final case whose wave has ended; back office before the end | | `404` | unknown case (including a final case whose wave has not started), session, thread or attachment | | `409` | thread or session ended (also at a wave's cap); round limit reached; late (timeout); final case already played | | `413` | request body over 64 KB | | `422` | invalid request or message - nothing happens, no round is used | | `429` | over a limit: calls per second (`Retry-After: 1` - retry), open sessions (close one first), the practice quota (`practice limit: …`, `X-Practice-Remaining: 0` - wait until `resets_at`) | Errors carry a readable reason: `{"detail": "…"}`.

# Tacto Negotiation Arena - starter kit

A Python client for the arena API, two example buyer agents that negotiate by e-mail, helpers that
read the suppliers' documents and price a term sheet, a runner that plays many cases in parallel,
`arena-sim` - a local simulator of the arena's API - and a read-only MCP server over the data
package. Read the brief first
(`../brief/brief.md`); the full API is in `../brief/api.md`. Code: MIT.

## Quickstart - first agent on the board in 15 minutes

You need Python 3.12 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/).

**1. Get your team's key** (one per team): open `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply`, enter your team name and a
contact e-mail, and show the match code it displays at the Tacto desk. Once an organiser approves,
the key appears **once** on that page - copy it and press "Got the key". Only that page (or its
link) shows it; lost it → ask the organisers to reset it. Keep it out of git.

```bash
cd starter-kit
uv sync --all-extras            # 2. install
cp .env.example .env            # 3. put ARENA_URL and your key (ARENA_API_KEY) into .env
uv run arena me                 # 4. your team and its practice quota
uv run arena cases              # 5. the practice cases (the 10 hosted ones are playable)
uv run arena play case:P01 -v   # 6. the naive agent negotiates one case
uv run arena board              # 7. you are on the practice leaderboard
```

Is the arena up? `curl $ARENA_URL/health`.

Step 6 prints the deal, your total cost `c_deal` against `c_open` and `c_best`, the case score,
and a **replay link**: every e-mail and the supplier's reasons for each move, in words. That is
the learning loop - play a practice case, read the replay, improve your agent, play
again. In practice your best score per case counts, so play a case again whenever your agent improves.
**Quota:** 200 practice sessions per team per rolling 24 hours. `arena play` and `arena run` print
how many are left; `arena run` plays only the hosted practice cases and stops starting new ones
once the quota is used up (a `429` there does not go away by retrying). Plan your runs.

**Now the LLM agent.** Download the data (`ARENA_DATA=data/package` in `.env`), choose a model in
`.env` (your own key), then:

```bash
uv run arena data                                          # unpacks data/package (and the Sunday release once public)
uv run arena play case:P01 --agent llm -v
uv run arena run --set practice --agent llm --parallel 8   # every hosted practice case, 8 at a time
uv run arena play case:D02 -v                              # the sandbox: 3 demo suppliers, no board
```

**Sunday 08:00:** run `arena data` again - it adds `data/release-sunday` (new news, letters, a
memo). `DataPackage` merges its facts and documents automatically; hidden cases may cite them.

## Hello World (local, 3 commands)

No key yet? Play a whole case against the local simulator - no network, no quota, no LLM costs.
The simulator's supplier is a plain script; the real ones are on arena.tacto.ai. After
`uv sync --all-extras` (step 2 above):

```bash
# terminal 1: the simulator (--data is optional: leave it out until you have run `arena data`)
uv run arena-sim serve --no-clock --data data/package
# terminal 2: a simulator key, then the naive agent plays case:S01
ARENA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 uv run arena register "Hello World" sim                  # prints an api_key
ARENA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 ARENA_API_KEY=<the api_key> uv run arena play case:S01 -v
```

It prints the deal, `c_deal` against `c_open` and `c_best`, the score and a replay link - open it
in your browser: the result on top, then every e-mail of the negotiation.

## Try it by hand (Postman, curl)

Feel the API before you put a model in front of it. On the real arena (practice and sandbox) the
60-second rule applies: three late replies in a row end the thread - too fast for typing. **By
hand, use the simulator first**, without the clock:

```bash
uv run arena-sim serve --no-clock --data data/package           # data/package from `arena data`; --data is optional
ARENA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 uv run arena register "Team Name" sim   # prints a simulator api_key
export SIM=http://127.0.0.1:8000 KEY=<the api_key>
```

Every call sends `X-API-Key: <key>`; every `POST` also `Content-Type: application/json` and a
fresh `X-Move-Id` (any unique string - the same id again returns the same answer). In Postman:
those headers, the body as raw JSON.

```bash
# 1. the cases: case:S01 has one supplier, sup:70270, and the negotiable fields unit_price, payment_days
curl -s "$SIM/v1/cases?set=practice" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"

# 2. open a session: the reply carries session_id (sim1 on a fresh simulator) and each supplier's quote e-mail
curl -s -X POST "$SIM/v1/sessions" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Move-Id: open-1" -d '{"case_id": "case:S01"}'

# 3. the supplier's opening e-mail: its term sheet (offer:70270-0) and the quote PDF to fetch
curl -s "$SIM/v1/sessions/sim1/threads/sup:70270" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"

# 4. your e-mail with an offer: the reply is the supplier's answer (status, term_sheets, claim_results)
curl -s -X POST "$SIM/v1/sessions/sim1/threads/sup:70270/messages" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "X-Move-Id: msg-1" \
  -d '{"message": {"subject": "Adapter piece HI", "body": "Thank you for your quote. We offer 15.50 EUR at 60 days.",
       "term_sheets": [{"terms": {"unit_price": 15.5, "payment_days": 60}}]}}'

# 5. read the reply in the thread, and the session state
curl -s "$SIM/v1/sessions/sim1/threads/sup:70270" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"
curl -s "$SIM/v1/sessions/sim1" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"
```

To close, send `{"message": {"action": {"type": "accept", "term_sheet_id": "offer:70270-1"}}}` (the
term sheet you take) or `{"message": {"action": {"type": "walk_away"}}}` to the same `messages` path;
the answer carries the result and score. The quote PDF: `GET $SIM/v1/sessions/sim1/attachments/att:70270-0-quote`.
The same calls work on the arena (`https://arena.tacto.ai`, your team's key, a practice case) - with
the clock running.

## The Live Final: waves, in parallel, within the cap

The final comes in 5 themed waves. A wave holds several hidden cases that appear when the host
starts it; play them all in parallel (up to 10 open sessions per key). Each wave has a hard
cap - **8 minutes** (the host may extend one) - and what is still open then ends without a deal.
Start the runner before the first wave and leave it running:

```bash
uv run arena run --set final --agent llm --parallel 10
```

It polls `GET /v1/cases?set=final`, plays every case of a new wave at once (one agent per case),
closes each case **90 seconds before its wave's cap** (read from the wave's `seconds_left`, so an
extension counts) - earlier if a round in that case took longer
(`play.closing_move`: the cheapest standing term
sheet that keeps the must-haves and beats your alternative, else walk away) and stops after the
fifth wave has closed. If it crashes, start it again: it picks up the sessions it had started.
In Python: `play_waves(client, new_agent)`. It reads only your own cases and sessions - during
the final your agent must not read the leaderboard, the screen or the event feed (`arena board`
is for you, not for the agent).

A supplier's reply can take up to about a minute; its time never counts against your 60 seconds,
and the client waits up to 180 seconds for a reply. The client paces itself below the
limit of 10 calls per second and retries dropped connections with the same `X-Move-Id`, so a
retry never sends a message twice. Rehearse with `arena run --set practice --parallel 10` (it counts against your quota) before
Sunday, from the machine and network you will use: every case should end well inside 8 minutes.

## Your own agent

An agent is any object with `decide(case, threads) -> {"supplier_id": …, "message": {…}}`.
`threads` holds every e-mail so far per supplier, oldest first; supplier attachments come with
their text under `"text"`. The message is an e-mail - subject, body, up to 3 term sheets - or an
action that closes the case:

```python
from arena_kit import ArenaClient, RemoteTable, complete_offer, play, total_cost
from arena_kit.docs import standard_terms
from arena_kit.play import latest, live_threads, standing


class Haggler:
    def decide(self, case, threads):
        sid = live_threads(threads)[0]
        events = threads[sid]
        sheet_id, terms = standing(events)  # the supplier's standing term sheet
        std = standard_terms(events)  # from its quote PDF: what closes if a field is missing
        if latest(events)["status"] in ("agreed", "final_offer"):
            return {
                "supplier_id": sid,
                "message": {"action": {"type": "accept", "term_sheet_id": sheet_id}},
            }
        ask = complete_offer(case, {**terms, "unit_price": terms["unit_price"] * 0.97})
        print("their C:", total_cost(case, terms, std), "ours:", total_cost(case, ask))
        return {
            "supplier_id": sid,
            "message": {
                "subject": case["title"],
                "body": "Thank you for your quote. Could you send us a cost breakdown?",
                "term_sheets": [{"terms": ask}],
            },
        }


print(play(RemoteTable(ArenaClient()), "case:P01", Haggler()))
```

| Module | What |
|---|---|
| `client.py` | `ArenaClient`: one method per endpoint (messages, threads, attachments, back office, `me`, ...); paced, safe retries; `practice_remaining` |
| `play.py` | `play()`, `play_all()`, `play_waves()` (the Live Final); `RemoteTable` - the hosted arena (practice, sandbox, final) |
| `cost.py` | the published cost function C with the category goal's rates, `supplier_value` for the relationship term, must-haves, term-sheet completion |
| `docs.py` | supplier documents to text (PDF, XLSX); a quote PDF to its offered, standard and fixed terms |
| `data.py` | the data package and the Sunday release: `facts.json`, read-only SQL, lookup by ID, documents, cases |
| `agents/naive.py` | anchors 10 % low, splits the difference, accepts early - the baseline |
| `agents/llm.py` | the model writes the e-mail and the term sheets from the case and the data it points to; code computes C, reads the documents, removes IDs that do not exist, and refuses bad accepts |
| `sim.py` | `arena-sim`: the public API on your machine, with one plain scripted supplier (below) |
| `mcp_server.py` | the MCP server below |

The LLM agent is a starting point, not a winner: it sees only what the case file points to.
Finding the data that moves a supplier is your job - the worked example below shows one way for
one kind of argument. Ideas beyond it: mine the notes and e-mails, read the suppliers' signals and
documents, send two or three term sheets to learn what a supplier values, ask its roles the right

alternative.

# Tacto Negotiation Arena - starter kit

A Python client for the arena API, two example buyer agents that negotiate by e-mail, helpers that
read the suppliers' documents and price a term sheet, a runner that plays many cases in parallel,
`arena-sim` - a local simulator of the arena's API - and a read-only MCP server over the data
package. Read the brief first
(`../brief/brief.md`); the full API is in `../brief/api.md`. Code: MIT.

## Quickstart - first agent on the board in 15 minutes

You need Python 3.12 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/).

**1. Get your team's key** (one per team): open `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply`, enter your team name and a
contact e-mail, and show the match code it displays at the Tacto desk. Once an organiser approves,
the key appears **once** on that page - copy it and press "Got the key". Only that page (or its
link) shows it; lost it → ask the organisers to reset it. Keep it out of git.

```bash
cd starter-kit
uv sync --all-extras            # 2. install
cp .env.example .env            # 3. put ARENA_URL and your key (ARENA_API_KEY) into .env
uv run arena me                 # 4. your team and its practice quota
uv run arena cases              # 5. the practice cases (the 10 hosted ones are playable)
uv run arena play case:P01 -v   # 6. the naive agent negotiates one case
uv run arena board              # 7. you are on the practice leaderboard
```

Is the arena up? `curl $ARENA_URL/health`.

Step 6 prints the deal, your total cost `c_deal` against `c_open` and `c_best`, the case score,
and a **replay link**: every e-mail and the supplier's reasons for each move, in words. That is
the learning loop - play a practice case, read the replay, improve your agent, play
again. In practice your best score per case counts, so play a case again whenever your agent improves.
**Quota:** 200 practice sessions per team per rolling 24 hours. `arena play` and `arena run` print
how many are left; `arena run` plays only the hosted practice cases and stops starting new ones
once the quota is used up (a `429` there does not go away by retrying). Plan your runs.

**Now the LLM agent.** Download the data (`ARENA_DATA=data/package` in `.env`), choose a model in
`.env` (your own key), then:

```bash
uv run arena data                                          # unpacks data/package (and the Sunday release once public)
uv run arena play case:P01 --agent llm -v
uv run arena run --set practice --agent llm --parallel 8   # every hosted practice case, 8 at a time
uv run arena play case:D02 -v                              # the sandbox: 3 demo suppliers, no board
```

**Sunday 08:00:** run `arena data` again - it adds `data/release-sunday` (new news, letters, a
memo). `DataPackage` merges its facts and documents automatically; hidden cases may cite them.

## Try it by hand (Postman, curl)

Feel the API before you put a model in front of it. On the real arena (practice and sandbox) the
60-second rule applies: three late replies in a row end the thread - too fast for typing. **By
hand, use the simulator first**, without the clock:

```bash
uv run arena-sim serve --no-clock --data data/package           # data/package from `arena data`; --data is optional
ARENA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 uv run arena register "Team Name" sim   # prints a simulator api_key
export SIM=http://127.0.0.1:8000 KEY=<the api_key>
```

Every call sends `X-API-Key: <key>`; every `POST` also `Content-Type: application/json` and a
fresh `X-Move-Id` (any unique string - the same id again returns the same answer). In Postman:
those headers, the body as raw JSON.

```bash
# 1. the cases: case:S01 has one supplier, sup:70270, and the negotiable fields unit_price, payment_days
curl -s "$SIM/v1/cases?set=practice" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"

# 2. open a session: the reply carries session_id (sim1 on a fresh simulator) and each supplier's quote e-mail
curl -s -X POST "$SIM/v1/sessions" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Move-Id: open-1" -d '{"case_id": "case:S01"}'

# 3. the supplier's opening e-mail: its term sheet (offer:70270-0) and the quote PDF to fetch
curl -s "$SIM/v1/sessions/sim1/threads/sup:70270" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"

# 4. your e-mail with an offer: the reply is the supplier's answer (status, term_sheets, claim_results)
curl -s -X POST "$SIM/v1/sessions/sim1/threads/sup:70270/messages" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "X-Move-Id: msg-1" \
  -d '{"message": {"subject": "Adapter piece HI", "body": "Thank you for your quote. We offer 15.50 EUR at 60 days.",
       "term_sheets": [{"terms": {"unit_price": 15.5, "payment_days": 60}}]}}'

# 5. read the reply in the thread, and the session state
curl -s "$SIM/v1/sessions/sim1/threads/sup:70270" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"
curl -s "$SIM/v1/sessions/sim1" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"
```

To close, send `{"message": {"action": {"type": "accept", "term_sheet_id": "offer:70270-1"}}}` (the
term sheet you take) or `{"message": {"action": {"type": "walk_away"}}}` to the same `messages` path;
the answer carries the result and score. The quote PDF: `GET $SIM/v1/sessions/sim1/attachments/att:70270-0-quote`.
The same calls work on the arena (`https://arena.tacto.ai`, your team's key, a practice case) - with
the clock running.

## The Live Final: waves, in parallel, within the cap

The final comes in 5 themed waves. A wave holds several hidden cases that appear when the host
starts it; play them all in parallel (up to 10 open sessions per key). Each wave has a hard
cap - **8 minutes** (the host may extend one) - and what is still open then ends without a deal.
Start the runner before the first wave and leave it running:

```bash
uv run arena run --set final --agent llm --parallel 10
```

It polls `GET /v1/cases?set=final`, plays every case of a new wave at once (one agent per case),
closes each case **90 seconds before its wave's cap** (read from the wave's `seconds_left`, so an
extension counts) - earlier if a round in that case took longer
(`play.closing_move`: the cheapest standing term
sheet that keeps the must-haves and beats your alternative, else walk away) and stops after the
fifth wave has closed. If it crashes, start it again: it picks up the sessions it had started.
In Python: `play_waves(client, new_agent)`. It reads only your own cases and sessions - during
the final your agent must not read the leaderboard, the screen or the event feed (`arena board`
is for you, not for the agent).

A supplier's reply can take up to about a minute; its time never counts against your 60 seconds,
and the client waits up to 180 seconds for a reply. The client paces itself below the
limit of 10 calls per second and retries dropped connections with the same `X-Move-Id`, so a
retry never sends a message twice. Rehearse with `arena run --set practice --parallel 10` (it counts against your quota) before
Sunday, from the machine and network you will use: every case should end well inside 8 minutes.

## Your own agent

An agent is any object with `decide(case, threads) -> {"supplier_id": …, "message": {…}}`.
`threads` holds every e-mail so far per supplier, oldest first; supplier attachments come with
their text under `"text"`. The message is an e-mail - subject, body, up to 3 term sheets - or an
action that closes the case:

```python

from arena_kit.docs import standard_terms
from arena_kit.play import latest, live_threads, standing


class Haggler:
    def decide(self, case, threads):
        sid = live_threads(threads)[0]
        events = threads[sid]
        sheet_id, terms = standing(events)  # the supplier's standing term sheet
        std = standard_terms(events)  # from its quote PDF: what closes if a field is missing
        if latest(events)["status"] in ("agreed", "final_offer"):
            return {
                "supplier_id": sid,
                "message": {"action": {"type": "accept", "term_sheet_id": sheet_id}},
            }
        ask = complete_offer(case, {**terms, "unit_price": terms["unit_price"] * 0.97})
        print("their C:", total_cost(case, terms, std), "ours:", total_cost(case, ask))
        return {
            "supplier_id": sid,
            "message": {
                "subject": case["title"],
                "body": "Thank you for your quote. Could you send us a cost breakdown?",
                "term_sheets": [{"terms": ask}],
            },
        }


print(play(RemoteTable(ArenaClient()), "case:P01", Haggler()))
```

I've read the brief and checked your setup. Here's where you stand and what to do next, in order.

## Where you are
- **This is the Tacto Negotiation Arena.** You build an AI buyer agent that negotiates by e-mail with the hosted supplier bots. It's scored on total cost in € (`score = (C_open − C_deal)/(C_open − C_best)`). The Live Final is Sunday at 12:00: 5 waves of hidden cases, 8 minutes each, with no human in the loop.
- **Done:** `uv sync` ran, and your arena key works (`arena me` returns team "Promptly Done" with 0 of 200 practice sessions used).
- **Not done yet:**
  - The data package hasn't been downloaded (there's no `data/package` folder).
  - `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is empty in `.env`, so the LLM agent can't run.
  - Your own repo (`tacto_challenge`) ignores the whole `negotiation-arena-kit/` folder, so none of your agent code would be submitted.

## Next steps

**1. Finish setup (about 10 minutes)**
- Put your key into `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in [.env](.env).
- Consider a faster model than `claude-opus-5-5`. Each message must go out within 60 seconds of the supplier's reply, and you'll run up to 10 cases in parallel. Sonnet at low effort is the safer choice for the final.
- Download the data:
```bash
uv run arena data
```

**2. Get a baseline on the board**
```bash
uv run arena play case:P01 -v
```
```bash
uv run arena play case:P01 --agent llm -v
```
Read the replay links. They show the supplier's reasons in words, and that's your main learning signal. Don't run all 10 hosted cases yet; the quota is 200 sessions per rolling 24 hours.

**3. Set up your own repo for the agent**
Put your agent in `tacto_challenge`, for example `agent/` importing `arena_kit` as a dependency, rather than editing inside the kit's git checkout. You'll need to submit a repo, a README and a commit hash, and the repo must never contain `.env` or keys.

**4. Build a better agent than `agents/llm.py`.** The brief's tips point to:
- **Prepare before opening a session**, since the 60-second clock starts then. For each case, use code to pull:
  - the supplier's cost drivers (`cost_drivers`) and index changes, giving citable `idx:` claims with exact figures
  - should-cost (`cost:`), past POs, scorecards and quality notifications
  - call notes, letters and news about that supplier
- **Read the supplier, don't just stack data.** Find what it wants: a cash-short supplier trades price for shorter payment days, and a near-monopolist may move on terms but not on price. That's in the notes and correspondence.
- **Let code do the maths and the LLM write.** Use `total_cost` to price every candidate term sheet, including the margin/relationship term for `stabilise` and `secure_supply` cases. Send 2–3 term sheets at once to learn what the supplier values.
- **Guard the close.**
  - Check the must-haves.
  - Read the quote PDF's standard terms before accepting.
  - Walk away when the alternative beats the deal.
  - In RFQs, cite rival quotes to the other bidders.
- **Don't leak** urgency, a budget, or the lack of an alternative.

**5. Iterate:** play, read the replay, fix, replay. Keep a small log of what moved each supplier type.

**6. Prepare for Sunday**
- After 08:00, run `uv run arena data` again to get the Sunday release.
- At 09:00, run the pre-flight on the machine and network you'll use for the final. Rehearse with `arena run --set practice --parallel 10`; every case should finish well inside 8 minutes.
- Before 12:00:
  - Submit the repo, commit hash, description and slides on ehl.gg.
  - Start the final run (command below), logging to a file, with the laptop on power and sleep disabled.
```bash
uv run arena run --set final --agent <yours> --parallel 10
```
- During the final, your agent must not read `/v1/events`, `/leaderboard`, `/screen` or `/results`.

Want me to start on step 3 (repo layout plus an agent skeleton with the preparation step) once your Anthropic key is in `.env`?

content.text:
Everything is run from the **`starter-kit/`** folder.

## 1. Add your OpenAI key
Open [starter-kit/.env](.env) and replace the LLM section (everything below `ARENA_DATA=...`) with:

```
LLM_PROVIDER=openai
LLM_MODEL=gpt-4.1-mini
LLM_API_KEY=sk-...your key...
```

Leave `ARENA_URL`, `ARENA_API_KEY` and `ARENA_DATA` as they are.

- **No `LLM_BASE_URL` needed.** The agent already defaults to `https://api.openai.com/v1` ([llm.py:74](arena_kit/agents/llm.py:74)).
- **Pick a fast model.** Each reply must go out within 60 seconds, and the kit cuts off the LLM call at 45 seconds, after which it falls back to the naive move. Slow reasoning models risk timing out, especially with 10 cases running in parallel.
- **`LLM_EFFORT` does nothing with OpenAI.** Only the Anthropic path reads it.
- **Keep the key out of git.** `.env` is already gitignored in the kit, so don't copy it into your own repo.

## 2. Download the data
```bash
cd ~/github/tacto_challenge/negotiation-arena-kit/starter-kit
```
```bash
uv run arena data
```
This unpacks to `starter-kit/data/package`, which matches `ARENA_DATA=data/package` in your `.env`. That path is relative, so always run `arena` commands from `starter-kit/`. Run the same command again on Sunday after 08:00 to get the Sunday release.

## 3. Baseline (same folder)
The naive agent needs no LLM:
```bash
uv run arena play case:P01 -v
```
Then the LLM agent, once the key is in:
```bash
uv run arena play case:P01 --agent llm -v
```
Your practice-board standing:
```bash
uv run arena board
```

Each `play` uses 1 of your 200 practice sessions and prints the score, `c_deal` against `c_open` and `c_best`, and a **replay link**. Open the replay, because it shows why the supplier did what it did.

Once both baselines run, tell me the scores (or paste the output) and I can start on your own agent.

content.text:
Keeping `negotiation-arena-kit/` in `.gitignore` is right. But the team still needs one shared setup, and the way to get that is to make your repo depend on the kit as a package, not to commit a copy of it.

## Why not commit the kit folder
- **It's someone else's git repo.** It has its own `.git` pointing at tacto-ai, so committing it inside yours creates a messy nested repo.
- **Tacto keeps pushing updates.** The log already shows three "Kit update" commits. A copied-in kit drifts out of date, and merging updates into it is painful.
- **The jury should see your work.** tum.ai runs a code agent over your repo, and a clean diff of your own code is easier to judge than your agent mixed into the starter kit.
- **The data doesn't belong in git either.** It's large, and `arena data` downloads it anyway.

## Recommended layout
```
tacto_challenge/                 ← your team repo
├── pyproject.toml               ← depends on arena-kit, pinned to a commit
├── uv.lock                      ← committed: everyone gets identical versions
├── agent/                       ← your buyer agent
├── run_final.py                 ← your runner (see below)
├── .env.example                 ← variable names only
├── .env                         ← gitignored
├── data/                        ← gitignored (arena data downloads here)
└── negotiation-arena-kit/       ← gitignored, optional local clone for reading docs and examples
```

Point the dependency at the kit's `starter-kit/` subfolder on GitHub:
```toml
[project]
dependencies = [
  "arena-kit[anthropic] @ git+https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit@<commit>#subdirectory=starter-kit",
]
```

Each teammate then sets up with: clone, `uv sync`, `cp .env.example .env`, add the keys, `uv run arena data`. They all get the same kit version, the `arena` CLI, and the same data. When Tacto ships a kit update, one person bumps `<commit>`, re-locks, and pushes.

## One thing this changes
`arena run --agent` only knows `naive` and `llm` ([cli.py:29](arena_kit/cli.py:29)). So your own agent needs a small runner script that calls `play_waves(client, new_agent)` for the final and `play(...)` for practice. That script is also what your submission README tells people to run.

## Keys across the team
- Each person uses their own LLM key in their own `.env`.
- There's only one arena key, and it's shared.
- The 200-session quota is per team, so agree on who runs practice batches.

Want me to set this up now (pyproject pinned to the current kit commit, the folder layout, `.env.example`, a runner script and a README stub)?

"""The naive buyer: anchors a little low, splits the difference, accepts early.

A baseline to beat, not a strategy: it ignores the data and the documents, never trades, never
asks and never walks away. One term sheet per e-mail.
"""

from ..cost import complete_offer, total_cost
from ..play import latest, live_threads, moves_left, standing


class NaiveAgent:
    def __init__(self, anchor=0.10, close_gap=0.01):
        self.anchor, self.close_gap = anchor, close_gap

    def decide(self, case, threads):
        # Talk to the supplier whose standing term sheet costs least.
        quoting = [s for s in live_threads(threads) if standing(threads[s])[1].get("unit_price") is not None]
        if not quoting:
            return {
                "supplier_id": live_threads(threads)[0],
                "message": {"action": {"type": "walk_away"}},
            }
        sid = min(quoting, key=lambda s: total_cost(case, standing(threads[s])[1]))
        events = threads[sid]
        sheet_id, terms = standing(events)
        accept = {
            "supplier_id": sid,
            "message": {"action": {"type": "accept", "term_sheet_id": sheet_id}},
        }
        theirs = terms["unit_price"]
        mine = [
            m["term_sheets"][0]["terms"]["unit_price"]
            for m in events
            if m.get("from") == "buyer" and m.get("term_sheets")
        ]
        if latest(events).get("status") in {"agreed", "final_offer"} or moves_left(case, events) <= 0:
            return accept
        if not mine:
            price = theirs * (1 - self.anchor)
        elif theirs - mine[-1] <= theirs * self.close_gap:
            return accept
        else:
            price = (theirs + mine[-1]) / 2
        return {
            "supplier_id": sid,
            "message": {
                "subject": case["title"],
                "body": "Thank you for your offer. We need a better price to go ahead.",
                "term_sheets": [{"terms": complete_offer(case, {**terms, "unit_price": price})}],
            },
        }

    def __init__(self, anchor=0.10, close_gap=0.01):
        self.anchor, self.close_gap = anchor, close_gap

                "message": {"action": {"type": "walk_away"}},
            }

content.text:
No, you don't need to write any code for the baseline. The starter kit already includes two working agents, and `arena play` runs the whole negotiation for you. You never type a price by hand.

## What `uv run arena play case:P01 -v` does
1. **Opens the case.** It creates a session, and the supplier sends its opening quote.
2. **Loops:** it asks the agent what to do, sends the agent's e-mail and term sheet, and waits for the supplier's reply ([play.py:142](arena_kit/play.py:142)).
3. **Ends when the agent accepts or walks away,** then prints the score and a replay link.

## How the agents choose prices
**Naive agent** (default; a fixed rule with no LLM, [naive.py](arena_kit/agents/naive.py)):
- It first offers the supplier's price minus 10%.
- Each round after that, it offers halfway between its last offer and the supplier's current price.
- It accepts once the gap is 1% or less, the supplier says `agreed` or `final_offer`, or it runs out of rounds.
- It never reads the data, never cites anything, and never walks away.

**LLM agent** (`--agent llm`, needs `LLM_API_KEY`):
- The model writes the e-mail and proposes the term sheets, using the case file and the data that file points to.
- Code computes the cost C, reads the supplier's documents, removes invented data IDs, and blocks bad accepts.

## Where your own code comes in
After the baseline. These two agents are the scores to beat. Your own agent is a class with one method, `decide(case, threads)`, which returns either the next e-mail with its term sheets or an accept/walk-away. The `play` loop runs it exactly as it runs these two, and that's where your strategy goes.

So go ahead and run the two `play` commands. Each one uses 1 of the 200 practice sessions.

content.text:
Yes, you can start building right away. I'd still run the naive baseline once first. It's 1 of your 200 sessions and about a minute, and it gives you three things you'd otherwise have to discover while debugging your own agent:

1. **A plumbing check.** It confirms the key, the network and the session flow all work before your own code is in the way.
2. **A number to beat.** `C_open`, `C_best` and the naive score on P01 show whether v1 actually helps.
3. **A first look at the real supplier.** The replay shows how it reacts to plain haggling. That shapes your strategy more than the brief does.

You can skip the `--agent llm` baseline. It's just a stepping stone.

## A first version that should beat the baseline
The kit agents ignore most of what the brief says matters. A v1 that should beat them:

1. **Prepare in code before opening a session** (no clock running):
   - Find the supplier's cost drivers and compute verified index changes, especially for drivers the letter blames that actually fell.
   - Pull should-cost, past PO prices, scorecards, and notes, letters and news about that supplier.
2. **Price every option with `total_cost`.** Build 2–3 term sheets that trade levers: price against payment days, effective date and contract length, the trade-offs the score rewards. Drop any that break a must-have or cost more than the alternative.
3. **Let the LLM only write the e-mail.** Give it the facts with their IDs, ask for one argument per sentence (at most 3 claims), and tell it never to leak urgency or a budget.
4. **Close with rules:**
   - Concede in steps toward an estimated floor.
   - Accept only if the deal beats the alternative and keeps every must-have.
   - Read the quote PDF's standard terms first.
   - Walk away when the alternative is cheaper.
5. **Use the replay** to see which arguments moved each supplier, and tune from there.

content.text:
0.58 is a solid starting point, and the replay shows a clear way to beat it. I pulled the session and priced some alternative term sheets with the kit's cost function.

## What the naive agent did on P01
| | |
|---|---|
| Supplier's opening quote | €138.55 from 1 Nov 2026 (current price €126.53) |
| Naive agent's offers | €124.70 → €131.00 → €133.75 → €134.82, then accepted the supplier's **€135.40**, 60 days, from **1 Nov 2026** |
| C_open / C_deal / C_best | €1,153,780 / €1,120,579 / €1,096,816 |

It bargained on price only, with no arguments and no data. The supplier conceded about €3 just to reward the movement.

## The big lever it missed: when the new price starts
`effective_date` is negotiable: 1 Nov 2026, 1 Jan 2027 or 1 Apr 2027. Any part bought before the new price takes effect is paid at the old €126.53. Pricing a few term sheets with `total_cost` (roughly; it leaves out the quality term):

| Term sheet | Score (approx.) |
|---|---|
| €135.40, Nov 2026, 60 days (what you got) | 0.61 |
| €135.40, Nov 2026, **90 days** | 0.74 |
| **€138.55 (the opening price!), Apr 2027**, 60 days | **0.87** |
| €139.80, Apr 2027, 60 days | 0.77 |
| €135.40, Apr 2027, 90 days | 1.0 (capped) |

Accepting the supplier's *opening* price with an April start beats everything the naive agent haggled for. Later start dates and longer payment terms are worth more than euros off the unit price. The supplier will charge something for them, but the scores above have room for that.

## Other things that matter for this case
- **The goal is `stabilise`.** Squeezing Brandlhuber below a 3% margin is charged at €15,470 per point, so pushing the price down hard can lose you money.
- **The letter blames energy, but electricity prices fell 3.7%** (`idx:PPI-D351`), a verified counter-argument. The supplier's own cited drivers (labour +2.7%, iron and steel +6.5%) did rise, so don't contest those.
- **Your fallback is weak.** The second source quotes €143.22 with a 70-day lead time against your 45-day need, so walking away is bad. Don't let the supplier find out.

## Two notes
- **You've played P01 three times** (3 sessions, all scoring 0.58). The naive agent behaves identically every time, so there's no point replaying it.
- **This is exactly what v1 should automate:** price every combination of the negotiable fields with `total_cost`, offer 2–3 term sheets that trade price against date and payment days, and back them with verified data.

Want me to build that now (repo setup plus the v1 agent), starting with P01 as the test case?

content.text:
No. You don't negotiate with everyone at once to get one big deal across the board. Each case is a separate, self-contained negotiation that ends in at most one deal.

## The unit is a case
A case is one buying problem for one part, for example "Brandlhuber wants +9.5% on volute casings". It comes with:
- **the trigger:** the supplier's letter, an expiring contract, or a request for quotes
- **your need:** for P01, 8,150 pieces a year for 1 year
- **which terms are negotiable:** for P01, unit price, start date of the new price, and payment days
- **your alternative:** what happens with no deal (for P01, a second-source quote at €143.22)
- **the supplier or suppliers** you talk to

The case ends when you **accept one supplier's offer** or **walk away**. Cases don't affect each other, and suppliers don't remember you between cases.

## Two kinds of case
**One supplier (most cases).** Of the 10 hosted practice cases, 9 have one supplier: P01–P04, P07, P08, P10, P11 and P18. You trade e-mails back and forth, up to 10 messages, then accept or walk away. It's a classic one-on-one negotiation.

**RFQ, 2–3 suppliers (P05 among the hosted cases).** Several suppliers quote for the same part in parallel e-mail threads.
- You can talk to all of them, in any order.
- You can play them against each other, for example by telling supplier B that A quoted €X (citing A's quote ID).
- You can only accept **one**, and accepting one ends the case. You pick a winner; you don't split the order.

## What a supplier is
Each supplier bot behaves like a person at a real company:
- **Hard limits:** it never goes below its cost floor, big moves need its boss's approval, and it gives nothing unless you move too.
- **Within those limits it acts like a person.** It reads your e-mail, checks any data you cite, and reacts to tone, arguments, threats and appreciation.
- **Each one has its own personality and situation,** and the data hints at what it is: a family foundry that values the relationship, a supplier short of cash that cares more about fast payment than price, a near-monopolist that barely moves.
- **Each reply** includes its current offer and a status: `open`, `final_offer` (push again and it may walk), `agreed`, or `walked_away`.

## The end goal: lowest total cost per case
Every case is scored by the total cost C of the deal you accept. C is more than the unit price; it also counts payment terms, start date, freight, quality and so on.
```
score = (C_open − C_deal) / (C_open − C_best)     clipped to 0 … 1
```
- **0** = no better than the opening quote. **1** = as good as any supplier would ever accept.
- **No deal** scores your alternative, which is sometimes the right call.
- **Your result** = the average score over all cases. In the Live Final that's 5 waves of hidden cases, each played once, all of a wave's cases in parallel within 8 minutes.

## So your agent's job, per case
1. **Read** the case and the data on that supplier.
2. **Work out** which terms are worth the most money and what this supplier wants.
3. **Negotiate by e-mail:** up to 3 term-sheet options per message, backed by data the arena can verify.
4. **Accept the cheapest acceptable offer** (in an RFQ, from the best supplier), or walk away if your alternative is cheaper.

P01 shows why the trade-offs matter. The naive agent haggled about €3 off the price and scored 0.58. Taking the supplier's *opening* price with a later start date would have scored about 0.87.

content.text:
The case decides which suppliers you can talk to, not your agent. Each case file lists its suppliers in `suppliers`, and every one of them sends its quote as soon as the session opens. In 9 of the 10 hosted practice cases there's only one supplier, so there's no choice to make. The choice only matters in an RFQ case such as P05, with 3 suppliers.

## How the current agents choose in an RFQ
`play()` asks the agent for **one message per step**, so each step the agent picks one supplier to write to (or to accept or walk away from).

- **Naive agent:** always writes to the supplier whose current offer has the **lowest total cost C** and ignores the others ([naive.py](arena_kit/agents/naive.py)).
- **LLM agent:** the model chooses. Its prompt lists every open thread with the supplier's status, current offer, the computed C and the messages left, and the model returns a `supplier_id` with its e-mail ([llm.py:128](arena_kit/agents/llm.py:128)). Nothing in the code tells it how to choose.

## What a better agent should do in an RFQ
1. **Keep every credible supplier in play.** Competition is your leverage, and once a supplier stops hearing from you, it's no longer a threat to the others.
2. **Rank suppliers by C, not by unit price.** Payment days, lead time, PPM (defect rate), freight and tooling all change the ranking.
3. **Use the rivals.** Cite the cheapest rival quote (its `quote:` or `offer:` ID with the price) to each of the others. That counts once per supplier. Citing a quote reveals it to that supplier, so only cite one that helps you.
4. **Accept the one with the lowest C** once offers stop improving, or walk away if your alternative is cheaper.

## A timing risk to check
The 60-second-per-message clock runs **per thread** from the moment the quotes arrive. If the agent writes only to one supplier, the others may count your silence as late replies, and three timeouts in a row end that thread. That means in an RFQ the agent should probably write to **all** suppliers each round. Let's check this on P05: play it once and look at the `timeouts` in each thread.

For v1, I'd rotate through the live threads each round and use code, not the model, to decide who gets which offer.

content.text:
## What an RFQ is
**RFQ = Request for Quotation.** You need a part, often a new one with no current supplier, so you ask several suppliers to quote and pick the best. In the arena, an RFQ case has 2–3 suppliers in parallel e-mail threads. You can negotiate with all of them, but you accept only one, and that ends the case.

**Example, P05 (pump shaft for the new HX series):**
- **Suppliers:** Dralveck, Hrvelec (Czech) and Fuchsreiter.
- **Need:** 4,200 shafts a year for 2 years.
- **You negotiate:** unit price, payment days and lead time.
- **Must-have:** lead time ≤ 42 days. A deal that breaks it scores 0.
- **Goal `leverage`:** use competition and data to push the price down.
- **No alternative supplier.** With no deal, everything is bought at the fallback price, so you nearly always want a deal here.

## The 7 case types
| Type | The situation | Typical levers |
|---|---|---|
| `price_increase` | A supplier announces a price rise ("+9.5% due to energy and wages") | contest it with index data, delay the start date, payment days |
| `renewal` | A framework contract is expiring | price, contract length, volume |
| `rfq` | New part, 2–3 suppliers compete | play rivals against each other, lead time, price |
| `bundling` | Combine several small parts with one distributor | volume for price |
| `raw_material` | Alloy or metal surcharges | an index clause or a fixed price, base price |
| `capacity` | The supplier is full or cuts your allocation | secure the volume and lead time, maybe pay a bit more |
| `quality` | The supplier's scorecard is red | defect-rate (PPM) commitment, chargebacks, an 8D corrective-action report |

Each case also has a **category goal** that sets how C is priced:
- **`leverage`:** push hard on price.
- **`stabilise` / `secure_supply`:** strategic or bottleneck parts. Squeezing the supplier's margin costs you.
- **`quality_first`:** defects are expensive.
- **`routine`:** simple, low-effort buys.

## How the cases are chosen
Tacto wrote all of them; you don't choose.

**Practice (now until Sunday 12:00)**
- **19 practice cases** (P01–P19), all readable through `arena cases`, so you can study every one.
- **10 are "hosted" (playable):** P01, P02, P03, P04, P05, P07, P08, P10, P11 and P18. Together they cover every case type.
- You choose which to play and how often, within **200 sessions per 24 hours**. Your best score per case counts on the practice board.
- The **sandbox** has two extra demo cases (D01 price increase, D02 RFQ) that don't count anywhere, so they're good for experiments.

**Live Final (Sunday 12:00): this is what ranks you**
- **Hidden cases** you've never seen, in **5 themed waves**. A wave's cases appear all at once, for every team.
- **8 minutes per wave.** Your agent plays all of that wave's cases in parallel, and anything still open at the cap ends with no deal.
- **One attempt per case,** no replays.
- **Same world, rules and case types as practice, but new suppliers and settings.** Up to a third combine supplier and case types that practice never shows. Some cite the **Sunday 08:00 data release**.
- **Score:** each wave scores 0–100 (the mean case score × 100), and the sum over the 5 waves (up to 500) decides the top 10, who then pitch to the jury.

## What this means for building the agent
Tuning to the 10 practice cases won't win. The final rewards an agent that **works out any case from its file and the data**: which levers are worth money (from `total_cost`), what this particular supplier wants (from its notes, letters and news), and when to close. Use practice to test that general logic: one or two runs per hosted case, read the replays, and fix the reasoning, not the case.
