content.text:
Almost. The "same code" part is right, but there are **5 waves, not 5 cases**, and each wave holds **several cases played at the same time**.

## The Live Final
```
Wave 1 (8 min) ──► Wave 2 (8 min) ──► Wave 3 ──► Wave 4 ──► Wave 5
  ├ case A ┐                            waves run one after another
  ├ case B ├ all in parallel
  ├ case C │
  └ …      ┘
```
- **Waves run one after another.** The host announces each wave's theme, then starts it.
- **Inside a wave, all its cases appear at once** and your agent plays them **in parallel**, up to 10 open sessions at a time. Nobody knows in advance how many cases a wave has.
- **8 minutes per wave.** Anything still open at the cap ends with no deal, which is why the cases have to run in parallel, not one by one.
- **Each case is played once.**

## Same code for every case: yes
The runner starts a **fresh agent object per case**, all from your code. Each one handles its case end to end: read the case and the data, negotiate, then accept or walk away. Cases don't share state, and suppliers don't remember you between cases.

That's why your agent can't be tuned to specific cases. The same code has to handle a price increase, an RFQ, a quality case or a capacity case correctly, including combinations it never saw in practice.

## In practice
- **One case:** `arena play case:P01`. Good for development: one session, read the replay.
- **All hosted cases in parallel:** `arena run --set practice --parallel 10`, a rehearsal of a final wave. It costs 10 sessions per run.
- Before Sunday, check that a full parallel run finishes **well inside 8 minutes** with your LLM. Ten cases at once means many LLM calls together, which can hit OpenAI rate limits or the 60-second-per-message limit.

content.text:
Yes, and that's already how it works: **one program, one agent per case.**

The runner (`play_waves` for the final, `play_all` for practice) starts a **separate agent object for each case** with `new_agent()`, and runs them side by side in a thread pool ([play.py:224](arena_kit/play.py:224)):

```
arena run --set final --parallel 10        ← one process on your laptop
 ├─ thread 1: Agent() ── case A ── its own supplier(s)
 ├─ thread 2: Agent() ── case B ── its own supplier(s)
 ├─ thread 3: Agent() ── case C ── …
 └─ … up to 10 at once
```

Each agent:
- sees **only its own case** and its supplier threads
- keeps its **own state**: what it has offered and what the supplier said
- runs the **same code** (your agent class), so you write the logic once

So you don't write "one agent juggling every case". You write an agent that solves **one case well**, and the runner runs as many copies as there are cases.

## Inside one RFQ case
An RFQ is different. **One agent** handles all 2–3 suppliers of that case, because it has to compare their offers, cite one supplier's quote to another, and accept exactly one. Separate agents per supplier couldn't coordinate that.

## Things to watch with parallel agents
- **The LLM rate limit.** 10 agents calling OpenAI at once can hit your account's per-minute limits. A slow reply risks the 60-second limit, and the agent then falls back to the naive move.
- **Shared read-only data is fine.** The data package is loaded once and shared, which is safe because nobody writes to it.
- **The API limit is handled.** The arena allows 10 calls per second per key, and the kit's client already paces itself below that.

content.text:
You start the program **once**, before 12:00, and it finds out by itself how many cases there are.

## What `arena run --set final` does
```
start (before 12:00, once)
  │
  ▼
loop every 5 seconds: GET /v1/cases?set=final
  │   before wave 1   → 403, keep waiting
  │   wave 1 starts   → the list now contains wave 1's cases (e.g. 6)
  │                     → one agent per new case, all in parallel
  │   wave 2 starts   → the list grows by wave 2's cases → new agents for those
  │   …
  ▼
after the 5th wave has closed → the program stops by itself
```
- **It discovers cases by polling.** Nobody tells you in advance how many cases a wave holds. When a wave starts, its cases appear in that list, and the runner starts an agent for each case it hasn't seen yet ([play.py:224](arena_kit/play.py:224)).
- **It runs once per case.** The arena allows only **one session per case**, so a second attempt is rejected (`409`).
- **It closes in time.** The runner reads each wave's `seconds_left` and makes every agent close its case about 90 seconds before the cap, accepting the best valid offer or walking away, so nothing is lost to the timeout.
- **It recovers from crashes.** If the program crashes, start it again: it picks up the sessions it already had open instead of starting new ones.

## What you write
Only the agent class: one case in, decisions out. Your runner script is a few lines:
```python
from arena_kit import ArenaClient
from arena_kit.play import play_waves
from agent import MyAgent

play_waves(ArenaClient(), MyAgent)   # MyAgent is the factory: one new agent per case
```
On Sunday you start that before 12:00, log to a file, keep the laptop awake, and don't touch it. No human in the loop is allowed.
